Nothing is producing. When should I give up & rip out my plants?
I’m in zone 9b (Sacramento, CA), and I’ve planted tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, green beans, and eggplant back in Spring according to this UC Davis Vegetable Planting Guide. Nothing produced well. Maybe a couple of green beans, and a handful of cherry tomatoes. Some tomatoes have been green since late June/ early July, some tomato plants haven’t produced anything including flowers, no cucumbers, and I have sunburnt peppers with dry brown patches. My eggplants are the same size as when I bought them as starts. No fruits or flowers. 


It’s been 90-100f degrees most days since July. My soil moisture meter says “moist” and I hand water plants when it indicates “dry” (every 2-3 days or so). 

I’m so annoyed. Should I just rip everything out and start focusing on a fall garden?

I have been getting keen on saving veggie scraps to use in soups, but have just stuck with the standard, onion skins, carrot ends, celery leaves, etc.  I would like to branch out but just wonder if anyone has tried (or just know of) veggies that throw off the taste of the stock in an undesirable way? ​

Edit:

Wow so this is my first post to kind of "take off" on reddit, I can now fully appreciate the phrase "RIP inbox" lol.

Here's my TLDR takeaway/thread highlights:

Some people have solid "do's and don'ts" that they recommend.

There were multiple mentions of [this guide](https://jenniferskitchen.com/cooking-tips/vegetables-to-include-or-exclude-from-vegetable-stock-or-broth) which looks pretty awesome and is now in my bookmarks. 

Some were of the opinion to use whatever and make it work, I think this post from u/undeadfred sums up the sentiment pretty well:

> It depends. Are you trying to make the best homemade stock possible or are you trying to reduce waste by using up scraps that would otherwise be thrown away. I’ve only done the latter, and I’ve never had a batch that turned out bad. Possibly that’s because of the vegetables I typically eat, though. I don’t know. But, in my experience, I’ve never had a bad batch of homemade stock. 

And there were also some interesting alternative ingredients mentioned, two standouts were fruits and this mention by u/StinkyCheeseWomxn and others:

> There is a product called Kitchen Bouquet that is basically a bottle of Maillard reaction. It gives soups and gravies this amazing umami flavor and richness. I always thought it was beef based but it is actually vegan; basically caramelized vegetables. Add it to your soup or stick and it will make it next level. [https://www.cannibalnyc.com/kitchen-bouquet/#:\~:text=Kitchen%20Bouquet%20is%20a%20vegan,rated%20as%20better%20than%20average](https://www.cannibalnyc.com/kitchen-bouquet/#:~:text=Kitchen%20Bouquet%20is%20a%20vegan,rated%20as%20better%20than%20average). 

There was also some good discussion of alternative ways to deal with veggie scraps that don't involve making broth.

Thanks everyone for the enlightening discussion!

I have a confession 
So I come from a family of foodies- like my mom/grandmas/aunts all won cooking contests back in the day before we had cooking shows- like my aunt won a $20K kitchen makeover my grandma won two years of chicken and a giant check made out of chocolate (nestle) my mom won a cow, yes a cow for the national beef cookoff. Anyhow just came from a family dinner and I was asked to bring a ceasar salad. 

As you can imagine the pressure is real especially cause even as I’m an adult I’m still one of the kids in the family and it’s a big deal to be assigned something other than napkins or ice 😂 

So I made the ceasar salad I make for me and my kid and I kinda feel like I got away with a crime because they all loved it and asked for the recipe but I can’t tell them, so I’m telling Reddit because it’s freaking delicious and maybe I’ll just tell them I used an old Martha Stewart or Ina Garten recipe or something haha

Recipe:

3 bags store bought ceasar kits
Take out the dressing and add the ceasar dressing to a jar with a healthy scoop of mayo, jarlic, juice of two lemons and pepper- shake and let marinate bonus if you have a jar of Olive Garden Italian dressing add a splash of that.
Cut up a couple Roma tomatoes finely diced
Five or six strips of bacon- sprinkle with cayenne and brown sugar and cook in the oven for peak carmelization then crumble

Lastly wash the bags of salad and chop up to get smaller peices- then assemble lettuce, dressing tomatoes, bacon, and the packets of parm and croutons sooooo good! I’m proud they liked it and ashamed it’s not totally homemade because that’s what they’re all about

Need advice on planting based on nutrition 
Hey, I'm thinking about jumping right into growing my first plants, being tomatoes and cucumbers but I want to choose the absolute perfect seed types. Now I don't know much about gardening, but I've been watching a ton of informative videos lately. I was just about to head to a nursery but then asked myself "which type of plant variety has the better nutritional value and is healthier to consume?". After trying to do some research, l'm now reading that fruits and vegetables aren't as nutritional as they were hundreds of years ago. So it leaves me wondering, in terms of choosing the healthiest breed of tomatoes/cucumbers, what can I do? As someone who lives in New Orleans, LA, I understand that there can be factors such as climate and disease that should lead me to picking the correct breed, so l'm just feeling a little lost and uncertain at the moment. My dream is to eventually grow many crops that are all specifically chosen to be the most nutritious breeds. Any advice or recommendations would be very much appreciated
